strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: generating dynamic graphs with structural, temporal, and rich textual attributes.
GDGB covers eight sizable datasets from diverse domains, including both bipartite and non-bipartite graphs, and provides node and edge text rather than only compressed features.
The distinction between transductive generation and the more challenging inductive generation of new nodes is useful for organizing future research.

The paper evaluates several LLM backbones, includes two dynamic graph generators and multiple DGNN baselines, and reports extensive supplementary results, prompts, dataset descriptions, and scalability measurements.
The proposed evaluation suite attempts to cover structural fidelity, textual quality, and joint graph-level fidelity rather than relying on a single statistic.
weaknesses: The graph-embedding metric is internally inconsistent. It is mathematically defined as cosine distance, for which lower is better, but Tables 10 and 46 and the associated conclusions treat larger values as better. The ablation claims likewise describe increased values as improvements, while many tables contain mixed or opposite trends. This directly undermines a central part of the evaluation.

The graph-embedding construction is insufficiently specified and may not be well-defined: textual strings and interaction histories of varying lengths are described as concatenated into vectors, randomly projected, and compared using a Frobenius inner product even when graphs have different node counts. The text encoder, alignment, projection dimensions, randomization protocol, and handling of unequal graph sizes are omitted.

The textual evaluation is weakly validated. A single GPT-based evaluator assigns highly saturated scores, often near 5.0, without a complete evaluator prompt, sample counts, repeated judging, uncertainty, human agreement, reference-based checks, or comparisons against established automatic metrics. The assertion that this procedure outperforms BERTScore is unsupported.

The TDGG discriminative evaluation is not defined precisely enough to interpret. It is unclear how generated edges are aligned with held-out ground-truth edges for Hit@k and edge classification, whether labels are compared against real labels or merely checked for consistency with generated text, and how active sources and candidate destinations are selected. Consequently, the unusually large classification gains over DGNNs are not convincing.

Baseline comparisons are not fully fair or diagnostic. GAG-General receives raw text and powerful pretrained LLM knowledge, whereas DG-Gen and VRDAG receive BERT representations and cannot generate text. Results also select the best of four LLM backbones without an analogous validation procedure, and omit simple temporal, preferential-attachment, retrieval, or text-conditioned heuristic baselines.

Claims that memory and reflection provide significant improvements are unsupported by statistical tests or repeated-run variance and are contradicted by numerous graph-embedding entries where the reported metric worsens. Sampling-based LLM generation is evaluated without random-seed sensitivity or confidence intervals.

The claimed textual quality of the datasets is supported mainly by average text length and downstream structural MMD. There is no systematic audit of missingness, duplication, noise, language coverage, leakage, factual accuracy, or semantic usefulness. The use of uncased English BERT on Chinese-origin datasets is also not explained.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the benchmark framing: many preprocessing and crawling decisions, metric implementation details, evaluator settings, monetary/API costs, and prompts for six of the eight domains are absent.

The data-governance discussion is inadequate. Several datasets contain user profiles, locations, usernames, reviews, or social-media interactions, yet privacy and consent are addressed only generically. The stated redistribution licenses—especially for Dianping and IMDb—require substantially clearer justification and may restrict the proposed public release.

Several conclusions are overstated. Passing a hand-set power-law criterion and obtaining MMD values below 0.3 do not by themselves establish high-quality generation, while the hub-node discussion interprets invented products as predictive future trends without prospective validation. Overall, the potentially valuable dataset contribution is not supported by a sufficiently sound and reproducible evaluation for acceptance.

strengths: The manuscript targets an underexplored and potentially important problem: generating dynamic graphs with textual node and edge attributes.
GDGB spans eight datasets, multiple domains, bipartite and non-bipartite structures, and both transductive and inductive settings.
The paper contains extensive experiments across several LLM backbones, conventional dynamic-graph models, ablations, and scalability measurements.
The task descriptions, pseudocode, dataset summaries, and generation prompt examples provide a useful starting point for future benchmark development.
weaknesses: The proposed graph-embedding metric is technically ill-defined. It concatenates raw textual and variable-length interaction histories without specifying their numerical encoding, alignment, padding, or ordering; random projection does not make Frobenius comparison between differently sized graphs valid. Moreover, the appendix defines rho = 1 - cosine similarity and states that lower is better, while the experiments interpret larger values as better. This directly undermines a central evaluation component.

Despite repeated claims of jointly evaluating temporal fidelity, no direct temporal metric is reported, such as inter-event-time, event-count, burstiness, or timestamp-distribution error. Temporal information is only folded into the unclear embedding metric.

The evaluation is vulnerable to temporal leakage. Node profiles include aggregate review counts, ratings, follower counts, citation counts, and historical activity statistics that may have been computed using the full datasets. The paper does not explain whether these attributes are reconstructed as of each evaluation timestamp. Such future-derived features could substantially inflate generation and prediction performance.

The task protocol is insufficiently specified and partly conditioned on privileged information. TDGG obtains node updates from the original graph, while IDGG fixes new-node counts from observed data. The construction of the matched ground-truth target, timestamp generation horizon, treatment of isolated nodes, and exact information available at each round are unclear.

Text quality is assessed only by a GPT-based judge using subjective criteria, without the complete evaluator prompt, sampling details, repeated judgments, uncertainty estimates, human validation, or comparison against real held-out text. Scores clustered near 4–5 suggest poor discrimination, and using a related GPT model as both generator and evaluator raises self-preference concerns.

The baseline comparisons are not convincingly fair. GAG-General benefits from pretrained LLM knowledge, detailed profiles, memories, and candidate retrieval, whereas DGNNs and graph generators are trained on only 1,000 edges. Results select the best of four LLM backbones without a stated validation-selection protocol, and baselines lack comparable access to raw text generation capabilities.

Claims that longer text establishes higher textual quality are unsupported. There is no systematic audit of correctness, duplication, missingness, noise, language distribution, temporal validity, or semantic usefulness, and the dataset construction/crawling procedures are not reproducible in sufficient detail.

Reported structural results lack repeated trials, confidence intervals, statistical tests, and sensitivity analyses for random sampling, LLM decoding, MMD bandwidth, graph size, and seed selection. Power-law validity is reduced to an ad hoc threshold and is not evidence of overall graph realism.

The claimed real-world predictive utility is unsupported. Generated hub products are described as potential future viral products, but no prospective or held-out forecasting evaluation shows that these synthetic hubs correspond to future outcomes.

The ethics and release discussion is inadequate for datasets containing usernames, locations, demographics, biographies, social posts, and reviews. The paper provides no concrete consent, anonymization, personally identifiable information removal, harmful-content filtering, or deletion procedure. It also does not reconcile redistribution with restrictive terms such as IMDB's personal/noncommercial-use conditions.

Several presentation errors further reduce confidence, including inconsistent timestamp statistics, a mistaken reference to Table 2 in the IDGG discussion, missing evaluator details, and strong language such as “groundbreaking” unsupported by the evidence. strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: generation of dynamic graphs with raw textual node and edge attributes.
GDGB has broad scope, covering eight sizable datasets, several application domains, and both bipartite and non-bipartite graphs.
The distinction between transductive generation with known nodes and inductive generation with newly created nodes is useful and could help standardize future research.
The paper includes extensive supplementary material, implementation details, prompts, multiple LLM backbones, structural baselines, ablations of memory and reflection, and scalability measurements.
The presentation is generally clear and well organized, and the dataset descriptions make the intended resource value easy to understand.
weaknesses: The graph-embedding metric has a central internal contradiction. It is defined as cosine distance, with lower values stated to be better, but the baseline tables and conclusions treat larger values as better. For example, GAG-General values around 0.66–0.83 are claimed to outperform VRDAG values around 0.01–0.11. The ablation conclusions similarly conflict with many reported values. This invalidates a major part of the evaluation unless the definition or all interpretations are corrected.

The proposed graph-embedding metric is insufficiently specified for reproduction. The paper concatenates textual strings and variable-length interaction histories into a 'node embedding,' applies an unspecified random projection, and then uses a Frobenius inner product between graph representations despite potentially different node counts. Text encoding, ordering, padding/alignment, projection dimensions, random seeds, and aggregation are not defined.

Textual evaluation relies exclusively on GPT-based judgments, apparently including evaluation of GPT-generated outputs, without human validation, evaluator agreement, evaluator prompts, sample counts, uncertainty, or robustness checks. Scores frequently approach 5.0, suggesting saturation and possible self-preference. Criteria adapted from role-playing, such as personality depth and immersive quality, are also not clearly appropriate for citation or revision graphs.

Temporal fidelity is not evaluated independently, despite being central to DyTAG generation. Degree and spectral MMD assess topology, while the only purported joint structural-temporal-textual measure is the problematic embedding metric.

The experimental protocol lacks repeated runs, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite stochastic LLM sampling, random walks, random projection, and random node sampling. Consequently, small ablation differences cannot support claims of significant improvement.

The discriminative comparison is difficult to interpret and potentially unfair: 'Ours' selects the best result among four LLM backbones and multiple configurations, apparently using test performance, while DGNNs receive only 1,000 training edges. The paper does not specify a validation-based model-selection protocol. Moreover, evaluating labels attached to generated edges is not clearly equivalent to predicting labels for fixed ground-truth edges.

The IDGG comparison does not establish semantic generation quality against prior models. VRDAG and DG-Gen output learned feature vectors rather than text, and those vectors are inserted directly into the proposed embedding computation, making representation spaces and metric inputs non-comparable.

Structural evaluation is narrow and sometimes overclaimed. Low degree/spectral MMD and a binary power-law heuristic do not establish realistic dynamic graph generation; no temporal inter-event, motif, clustering, component, assortativity, novelty, memorization, or downstream-utility analyses are provided.

Dataset quality is mostly argued using average text length and improvements from adding BERT features. Text length is not a reliable measure of semantic quality, and there is no systematic annotation audit, missingness analysis, leakage analysis, deduplication assessment, or comparison of information content.

Releasing scraped user profiles, reviews, social-media interactions, and derived texts raises privacy, consent, copyright, and licensing questions. The appendix itself quotes restrictive non-commercial IMDB terms, yet the paper proposes redistribution through a benchmark. The broader-impact discussion does not adequately resolve these issues.

GAG-General appears to be a moderate extension of the prior GAG framework, while the claimed practical conclusions—such as identifying future viral products—are speculative and unsupported by forecasting or real-world validation.

Overall, the resource could become valuable, but the metric inconsistency, under-specified evaluation, questionable comparison protocol, and unresolved data-governance issues are too substantial for acceptance in the current form.

strengths: The paper targets an underexplored and potentially important problem: generation of dynamic text-attributed graphs with jointly evolving structure, time, and text.

GDGB is broad in scale and domain coverage, comprising eight bipartite and non-bipartite datasets with node- and edge-level text. The dataset descriptions, licenses, statistics, prompts, and implementation details are extensively documented.
The TDGG/IDGG distinction is intuitive and useful, particularly the explicit treatment of new-node generation in IDGG.
The evaluation attempts to cover complementary dimensions, including topology, textual quality, temporal information, downstream utility, scalability, and limited human assessment.
Experiments span four LLM backbones, several dynamic graph and DGNN baselines, memory/reflection ablations, downstream tasks, and semantic-drift analysis.
weaknesses: The proposed graph-embedding metric is insufficiently defined and internally inconsistent. The text describes concatenating raw textual attributes and variable-length histories before random projection, but does not specify text encoding, dimensional alignment, node ordering, or how the Frobenius inner product is computed for graphs with different node sets. Moreover, the equation defines a cosine distance for which lower is better, whereas the tables use an upward arrow and interpret larger values as better. This directly undermines a central evaluation axis and several claimed improvements.

The textual evaluation is not adequately validated. A GPT-based evaluator—apparently using stochastic generation settings—is also used to evaluate outputs from a GPT generator, creating possible self-preference. Scores frequently approach 5.0, yet no repeated-evaluation variance, inter-evaluator agreement, alternative judge, or correlation with human judgments is reported. The small human study gives only averages and omits sampling granularity, annotator agreement, uncertainty, and per-criterion results.

Structural evaluation is narrow and sometimes misinterpreted. Degree/spectral MMD and a binary power-law heuristic do not establish temporal fidelity or realistic graph evolution. The paper labels graphs as high quality based on thresholds even when several MMD values are substantial, while the MMD bandwidth and important implementation choices are unspecified.

Baseline comparisons are not convincingly fair. Existing generators cannot produce text, yet the joint embedding comparison incorporates their numeric representations differently from GAG-General's text. GAG-General results are selected as the best among four LLM backbones, DGNNs are deliberately trained on only 1,000 edges, and results generally lack multiple-generation runs, uncertainty, or significance tests. Consequently, claims of significant or groundbreaking superiority are not supported.

The benchmark protocol remains ambiguous about chronological target construction, access to future node attributes, candidate sampling, and the precise ground-truth graph used for comparison. TDGG samples nodes from the full node set during generation, raising leakage concerns unless the information available at every timestamp is specified carefully.

Several conclusions are stronger than the evidence. Different generated hub nodes are presented as potential future viral products without predictive validation, and downstream augmentation gains do not rule out changes in sample size, leakage, or synthetic duplication as explanations.

Ethical and release considerations are too cursory for datasets containing usernames, user profiles, appearance traits, reviews, and social interactions. The paper does not document anonymization, consent, personally identifiable information filtering, or model-regurgitation safeguards. Redistribution rights are also unclear for resources such as IMDb and crawled platform content.

The benchmark could become useful, but the metric validity, protocol clarity, evaluation reliability, and privacy/licensing issues are substantial enough that the current evidence does not meet the acceptance standard of a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper targets an underexplored and potentially important problem: generation of dynamic graphs with rich node and edge text.
GDGB covers eight datasets, multiple domains, bipartite and non-bipartite graphs, and provides extensive dataset descriptions, prompt templates, and supplementary experiments.
The proposed TDGG/IDGG distinction is intuitive, and evaluating structural, temporal, and textual properties together is directionally valuable.
The experiments include multiple LLM backbones, several dynamic-graph baselines, ablations of memory and reflection, scalability measurements, downstream evaluations, and a small human study.
weaknesses: A central evaluation metric is not technically well-defined. The graph-embedding construction concatenates raw text, timestamps, and variable-length histories without specifying their numerical encoding, padding, node alignment, or how Frobenius similarity is computed when graphs have different node counts. Moreover, the paper defines rho as a distance for which lower is better, while all result tables label the metric as higher-is-better and interpret larger values as superior. This directly undermines a substantial portion of the conclusions.

The claimed holistic temporal evaluation is weak. There is no convincing standalone metric for timestamp distributions, inter-event times, ordering, or temporal motifs; temporal fidelity is largely delegated to the underspecified embedding metric.

The LLM-based textual evaluation is poorly validated and mismatched to the benchmark. Its role-playing criteria, such as personality depth and immersive quality, are questionable for citations, Wikipedia revisions, and actor collaborations. GPT is both a generation backbone and the sole automatic judge, no reference-based factuality evaluation is provided, and evaluator variance or bias is not studied.

The small human evaluation lacks essential methodological information, including annotator recruitment or expertise, assignment design, per-condition sample counts, uncertainty, and inter-annotator agreement. Averaged scores alone do not validate the automatic evaluator or support broad realism claims.

Several comparisons are not fair or diagnostic. DGNN baselines are deliberately trained on only 1,000 edges from datasets containing up to millions of edges, while the transductive LLM framework can access node identities and textual profiles from the broader graph. The paper then attributes baseline weakness to limited generalization. Reported 'Ours' values also select the best result among four LLM backbones, creating oracle model-selection bias.

Generation-baseline comparisons are reported on only three of the eight datasets and emphasize metrics favorable to the proposed method. Feature-based baselines cannot generate raw text, so the comparison does not cleanly separate differences in task capability from generation quality.

The experiments provide little evidence about statistical reliability. Stochastic LLM generation apparently uses one run with temperature 0.8, but most core tables report no confidence intervals, repeated-run variation, or significance tests. The memory/reflection ablations are also inconsistent across datasets and metrics despite being summarized as broadly beneficial.

The benchmark's split and ground-truth construction are insufficiently specified. It is unclear precisely which temporal segment constitutes each target graph, how future-node information is excluded, how candidate nodes are sampled, and whether the target size and node-arrival rates leak statistics from the held-out continuation.

The paper makes unsupported application claims. Structurally plausible synthetic hub nodes are described as potential future viral products, and generated graphs are proposed for forecasting market trends or misinformation, without evidence that synthetic entities correspond to future real-world outcomes.

Dataset governance raises serious concerns. The benchmark redistributes or derives sensitive user profiles, locations, appearance attributes, reviews, and social-media text, yet the ethics statement only gestures at anonymization without documenting actual procedures, consent, personally identifiable information removal, or bias analysis. The stated IMDB terms also appear restrictive, and the provenance of licenses attributed to scraped or third-party datasets is not adequately established.

The claimed novelty is diluted because much of the dataset contribution repackages existing public sources, while GAG-General is an extension of GAG. The paper does not sharply establish which algorithmic components are new or compare against simpler non-agent and retrieval/template baselines.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the extensive appendix: exact model/API versions, random seeds, sampling details, evaluator repetitions, computation and monetary costs, failure rates, and preprocessing decisions are incomplete. Overall, the central metrics and comparisons do not provide reliable enough evidence for the paper's strong claims.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem and offers a broad benchmark contribution: eight sizable text-attributed dynamic graphs spanning multiple domains, both bipartite and non-bipartite structures, and two clearly motivated transductive/inductive generation tasks.

The empirical study is unusually extensive, covering four LLM backbones, established dynamic-graph generation and DGNN baselines, memory/reflection ablations, scalability, semantic drift, downstream utility, and a small human evaluation.
The datasets, task definitions, prompts, implementation details, and licenses are documented in a substantial appendix, and the manuscript is generally clear and visually polished.

The inclusion of structural, temporal, textual, and downstream evaluations is directionally valuable, and the reported results suggest that text-rich graph data can support useful generative research.
weaknesses: A central proposed metric is technically inconsistent and insufficiently specified. The graph-embedding section defines rho as one minus cosine similarity and states that lower is better, whereas the experiments mark higher values as better and interpret them accordingly. Moreover, it is unclear how textual strings become compatible vectors, how variable-node graph matrices are aligned for a Frobenius inner product, and how randomness in the projection is controlled or validated.

Evaluation fairness and statistical reliability are weak. Several headline tables select the best result among four LLM backbones for the proposed method, while each competing generator receives a single result; baselines are trained on only 1,000 edges, VRDAG can generate a different graph size, and the comparison cannot assess raw-text generation by competing methods. Most generative results lack repeated-run variance or significance analysis despite stochastic sampling and temperature 0.8.

The textual evaluation relies predominantly on a GPT judge, including evaluation of GPT-generated outputs, with the same stochastic decoding settings used for generation. The criteria are adapted from role-playing and are not convincingly validated for graph attributes. The human study is only described as five annotators assessing 50 samples, without per-dataset sample accounting, agreement statistics, recruitment protocol, or uncertainty estimates.

The structural evidence is not sufficiently rigorous: power-law validity is treated as a general quality criterion without establishing that every reference graph follows that law, MMD bandwidth and spectral construction details are incomplete, and evaluations mainly use 2,000- or 10,000-edge prefixes despite datasets containing up to millions of edges.

The data-governance discussion is inadequate for a benchmark intended for release. The datasets include usernames, social posts, regions, appearance attributes, biographies, reviews, and citation text, yet the ethics statement only mentions anonymization as a hypothetical mitigation and gives no concrete de-identification, consent, privacy, or sensitive-attribute protocol. Redistribution rights also need stronger substantiation, particularly for IMDB, Dianping, crawled Wikipedia content, and copyrighted paper abstracts/citation sentences.

Some practical claims exceed the evidence. Structurally plausible synthetic hub nodes do not demonstrate an ability to forecast future viral products, and similar downstream scores on independently trained synthetic graphs do not by themselves establish faithful substitution for real data. Overall, the benchmark idea is promising, but central metric validity, comparison design, and data governance require substantial correction before top-tier acceptance.
